threat_assessment:
The table sees a four-mana Wizard, a fistful of Elves, and 36 Forests. Their read: fair stompy deck, ramping politely, no combo — and the record agrees with them. Zero contained combos, no game changers, a bracket floor of 1 against a target of 3. On paper you are the most ignorable deck at the table. Keep it that way. That paper is your camouflage, and your whole early game is spent keeping it accurate.

Your interaction is the untapped Forest. Stack 001 is the engine: Radagast's discount-and-flash resets every turn, so a four-player round hands you four windows and Wood Elves costs one green mana on an opponent's end step. So stop tapping out. Two open green is Frostfang, or Heroic Intervention, or nothing at all, and the table must price all three. Yeva widens the window into a door: with her out, every green creature spell in your hand has flash — the one-a-turn cap is gone, and only the {2} discount still belongs to the first spell each turn. Glademuse turns the discipline into income, a card for every cast made off-turn — that is you, up to four times a round (she pays an opponent's flash deck the same, so price that before she lands). The card they cannot see does the deterrence work — your job is only to hold it back and pass.

Spring the first trap early and make it cheap for you, expensive for them. Stack 002 is the lesson plan: Frostfang flashed after blockers are declared turns damage already lined up into deathtouch, and one unblocked 1/1 pays you two cards on the way out. A player who loses two attackers to open mana stops attacking you for the rest of the night. That is the point of the trade — you are not buying creatures, you are buying a reputation.

Three signals flip you from ignored to archenemy, and you control all three. A fifth body — because everyone can count to Craterhoof. A visible finisher — Chord of Calling mana held up with a big board is an announcement, so do not hold eleven mana ostentatiously unless you intend to use it. And Selvala — she actually reads friendly, since she offers everyone draws; let them believe it, and do not lead her into open removal without a reason, because she is your only card of her class and the sim finds her in barely one game in six.

Do not pivot at four bodies. Stack 003 did the arithmetic: Craterhoof over four other bodies is 36 unblocked into one seat — loud, board-committing, and not lethal from 40. The fifth body clears the bar. The count is the trigger: five bodies plus a finisher in hand, and not before. A telegraphed pivot that falls four short is how a deflection deck elects itself archenemy for free.

Be honest about your own clock. The sim measures 3.77 bodies by turn six — the fifth does not arrive until about turn eight — and the finisher in hand 42% of the time. All floors, since it models neither the discount nor a single flash cast, but respect the shape: your pivot is usually not ready on turn six, so do not start acting like the threat on turn five. Every turn you look like the ramp deck running slightly behind, someone else eats the removal.

And when the count is right, embrace it completely. Flash the fifth body in on the end step before your turn — it swings that same turn, the haste-equivalence stack 006 verified — but cast the Behemoth in your own main phase. Stack 005 killed the cuter line: his pump dies at that end step's cleanup, so an end-step Craterhoof is a wrath-dodge, never a kill. Untap, cast, and point everything at the seat that can rebuild interaction fastest, with Heroic Intervention or Tyvar's Stand held for the vote you just called. There is no radar to be under once the Behemoth resolves, and you do not need one: you counted, they didn't. Four verified stacks and ten thousand goldfish runs say the plan is sound — now go play the games that prove it.
matchups:
Sort the table by one question: who can afford to ignore your open mana? The seats that can't will slow down and play worse. The seats that can are the ones these notes are for.

The flier deck reads your 36 Forests and books the win — green cannot touch the sky, everyone knows it. Let them keep believing it. Whiptongue Hydra destroys every flier on the battlefield when he enters and grows a counter per corpse, and through Radagast's window he is a {3}{G} instant-speed air wipe. So the coaching is patience: do not fire him at two birds. Let the sky overextend, then flash him in after they commit to the attack and collect the whole board. Until he turns up, the fort holds itself — Hornet Queen's five deathtouch fliers make every swing at you a losing trade, Arasta and Dawn's Light Archer block at reach, and the Archer flashes in as a surprise blocker off two open mana. Warg Tactics is still there for the one flier that must die at instant speed — the commander, the engine piece — and Pick Your Poison's flying mode fires only when their best flier is their only flier. Keep your own clock on the ground with Toski and Frostfang drawing off every connect, and make the sky player explain to the table why attacking you cost them their air force.

Against aggro you are the control seat. Stack 002 already wrote the sign on your lawn — attack here and everything you lined up dies to a flashed Frostfang. Show it once, then let two open Forests do the job the card used to. Radagast's 2/5 blocks the early turns for free, and Guardian Augmenter flashes in to make him a hexproof 4/7 the moment someone tries to break the wall. Let the aggro seat spend itself into the other two players, then pivot the turn you stabilize — every passive turn past stable is a free draw step for somebody else.

Against sweeper control, fear the wrath early and welcome it late — the crossover card is Fecundity. Before your engines land, commit exactly as much board as wins before the sweeper arrives and not one body more. After Fecundity, the math flips: stack 004 verified that a Day of Judgment over your board pays you a card per creature — four wakes for you against their one — while Toski stands there indestructible and even Radagast's death is seen before he leaves for the command zone. Your rebuild is a feature, not a scramble: Radagast's first recast is six mana in a deck that finds ramp by turn six in 92% of runs, so redeploy worst-first, hold the finisher for their second sweeper, and flash the rebuild on end steps where a sorcery-speed wrath can never quite catch it — the one job stack 005 proves end-step deployment does best.

Against combo you are the beatdown, full stop — you lose every long game against inevitability. The toolkit is short: the clock, Collector Ouphe, Veil of Summer — and Deathgorge Scavenger when their engine lives in a graveyard, since he is a metronome body that eats the key card on the way in. Flash Ouphe in through Radagast's window on the combo player's own turn — stack 001 says the discount and the flash are live there — and hold Veil for the turn they point removal at Ouphe or disruption at your hand. Then be honest about the clock: stack 003 says one alpha strike takes one seat, not three, so the moment their proximity beats every board in sight, rank them archenemy and point all five bodies at the combo player, not the open one.

Against the artifact table you get to be the tax collector. Collector Ouphe switches off every activated mana rock at the table while your 36 Forests never notice he exists. Boseiju, Who Endures kills the key piece from your hand, and Life from the Loam brings it back — dredge Loam off any of your constant draw triggers, return Boseiju, channel again, with the cost shrinking for each legendary creature you control until it is one green mana per shot. Add Indrik Stomphowler, Caustic Caterpillar, Wickerbough Elder, and Nantuko Vigilante as bodies that double as answers, and their engine pays you rent every turn it tries to restart. That is nine removal-class cards pointed at the one table that must respect all of them — collect.
how_it_wins:
The table sees mono-green and waits for the turn you tap out. That turn never comes. Radagast makes your first creature spell each turn cost {2} less and lets you cast it at instant speed — and "each turn" means all four of them, verified to the letter in stack 001, where Wood Elves cost a single {G} on an opponent's end step. Pass with mana open and deploy in whichever window hurts the table most — and when Yeva, Nature's Herald lands, the cap comes off: every green creature spell gains flash, leaving Radagast's once-per-turn clause binding only the discount.

The open mana is never just a bluff — a trap is in hand by turn six in 91% of games, so the table has to respect it every time. Ohran Frostfang flashed in after blockers are declared hands your attackers deathtouch in time for damage: on the record, a 1/1 killed a 6/6 and the turn drew two cards (stack 002). Fecundity turns their wrath into your hand — four cards off a Day of Judgment while indestructible Toski just stands there (stack 004). Attacking you is bad, removing you is bad, wrathing you is bad.

The kill is arithmetic, so do the arithmetic — and cast it at home. Craterhoof over four bodies is 36, four short of a 40-life seat (stack 003); over five bodies it is exactly 40 into one seat, and the verified line is your own precombat main, haste carrying the attack (stack 005). Flash the Hoof on an end step and the pump dies at that turn's cleanup — legal, and it kills nobody. The end step is for bodies, not finishers: everything you flash there wakes up attack-ready on your turn (stack 006).

The goldfish hands you floors, and your job is to beat them. Radagast lands turn four on average and by six in 94% of games; a metronome body is drawn by six in 94.5% of games; the average board is 3.8 bodies at turn six — short of the five the kill needs. The sim models neither the discount, nor flash casts, nor the ramp auras, so the real numbers climb every time you use a window. Use the windows.

combo_lines.001:
The case turns on two words: "each turn." The printed template "each of your turns" exists, and Radagast does not use it — so the count of creature spells you have cast zeroes at every untap, yours and theirs alike, a turn being a structural unit every player takes (CR 500.1, CR 102.1). One candour the record keeps and this column repeats: no single rule states that an each-turn count resets. The holding is derived from the ability's text plus the definition of a turn, and the checker judged the derivation sound exactly as hedged.

What resolves: Wood Elves for {G} on an opponent's end step, both halves of the ability — discount and as-though-flash — riding the same first spell (CR 601.3d, CR 601.2f), the fetched Forest entering untapped because it is put, not played (CR 305.4). Plain English: four windows per round in a four-player pod, one spell per window, and your second creature spell in any turn gets nothing.
combo_lines.002:
The clause that decides this is CR 604.2: a static ability functions from the moment its permanent is on the battlefield. Nothing asks whether Ohran Frostfang was present when attackers were declared — attacking status persists until the creature leaves combat or combat ends — so deathtouch attaches to damage already lined up. Toski's single point destroys the 6/6 as a state-based action (CR 704.5h); the 6 coming back is ignored outright, indestructible reading the lethal-damage check out of existence (CR 702.12b).

On the draws the record is exact. One creature dealt combat damage to a player, and two separate abilities each saw that one event once (CR 603.2): two cards, not four. The holding: the trap is real, the snake pays you for springing it, and the record supports nothing wider.
combo_lines.003:
The controlling rule is CR 608.2h: X is read once, when the effect applies, and Craterhoof Behemoth is on the battlefield to be counted — five creatures, +5/+5, trample. The arithmetic is the exhibit: 7 + 6 + 6 + 7 + 10 makes 36, against a seat on 40. The holding is negative and this column will not soften it: not lethal. The seat survives on 4.

The record allows one sentence past the miss: a fifth body on the battlefield before the trigger makes X six and the attackers six, which clears 40. On where that fifth body comes from, the record is silent — it prices the bar, not the route.
combo_lines.004:
Two clauses carry this one. Fecundity's trigger reads "a creature," unqualified — the record confirms it fires for every seat's dead, the drawback accepted in full (CR 603.2c, one event, seven occurrences). And CR 111.7's own parenthetical: a token's zone-change triggers fire before the token ceases to exist, so the Insect's death pays out like any other.

The count on the record: you draw 4, the two-creature seat draws 2, the wrath's own caster draws 1, the creatureless seat draws 0. Two footnotes worth their ink. Toski, indestructible, never dies and so never pays anyone (CR 702.12b). And Radagast genuinely dies before the command-zone move — that move is an optional state-based action after the fact (CR 903.9a) — so his death is one of your four. The wrath resolves, and yours is the largest hand at the table.
combo_lines.005:
The ruling everyone wants to skip is CR 514.2: every "until end of turn" effect ends at the cleanup of the turn that made it — that turn, not yours. So the record splits this line cleanly in two. The ambush cast is legal in every particular: the conditional flash (CR 601.3d), Castle Garenbrig's six activated mid-cast as a mana ability (CR 605.3a, CR 601.2g), all six restricted {G} landing on a creature spell (CR 106.6). And the pump it buys dies at that turn's cleanup, so the next morning's attack is 10 unpumped power. It kills nobody.

The verified kill is the unglamorous one: the same mana in your own precombat main, X counting six, haste carrying the fresh Behemoth — 40 trample damage, exactly lethal to one 40-life seat (CR 704.5a), per seat and never the pod. What the flash cast retains is defensive: a sorcery-speed wrath exists only in its caster's main phase (CR 117.1a), so the end step before your turn is the last safe moment to deploy. The holding: flash the Hoof to dodge, cast him at home to kill.
combo_lines.006:
One rule decides both prongs: CR 302.6. The attack clause and the tap-ability clause read the same test — continuous control since YOUR most recent turn began — and a creature entering on the end step before your turn predates that clock. Sakura-Tribe Elder, flashed for {G}, may attack at dawn and could activate any tap ability it had; the two permissions are exactly the pair haste grants (CR 702.10b, CR 702.10c), obtained by timing instead.

Two precisions the record keeps. The equivalence holds only from your turn onward — during the opponent's turn itself the arrival still fails the test, where a hasty creature would not. And the Elder's own sacrifice ability carries no tap symbol, so CR 302.6 never restricted it at all: it could have been activated the moment the spell resolved. The holding: the metronome's end-step bodies are never summoning-sick on the turn you need them.
combo_lines.007:
The clause is CR 109.2b: a description containing the word "spell" means a spell of that description on the stack. Chord of Calling on the stack is an instant, never a creature spell — and from that one clause, three refusals follow. Radagast's discount does not apply, and the turn's window is not consumed. Castle Garenbrig's six restricted {G} cannot pay for it (CR 106.6) — though the Castle's plain {T}: Add {G} could, a distinction the record insists on. Beast Whisperer does not draw.

The fourth refusal has its own clause: the fetched creature is put onto the battlefield, not cast (the glossary's definition of "cast"), so nothing that triggers on casting fires for Selvala's arrival either (CR 603.6a governs what does). Two figures close the record: X must be at least 3, because Selvala's mana value is 3 and Chord finds X or less; and having entered on the end step before your turn, she taps for mana on it (CR 302.6 — the stack 006 boundary). The holding: Chord refuses every gift and still does the one thing this deck cannot otherwise do at instant speed.

card_roles.Radagast of Rhosgobel: The clock the whole deck ticks to: your first creature spell each turn costs {2} less and casts at instant speed, and "each turn" means all four of them (stack 001). Spend a window every turn — a round where you only act on your own turn wasted three.
card_roles.Llanowar Elves: Turn-one Elves is turn-three Radagast — the sim lands him on three in about a third of games, almost always off a dork. Late, it is still a body toward five, and in stack 002 this exact 1/1 drew two cards.
card_roles.Elvish Mystic: Llanowar Elves' second copy. Same instruction: turn one, every time.
card_roles.Fyndhorn Elves: The third copy of the same card. Eight dorks is redundancy doing its job — play whichever one you drew.
card_roles.Birds of Paradise: The dork that stays home. Zero power means it never attacks; it taps, it blocks a flyer, and it counts under Craterhoof's X.
card_roles.Devoted Druid: Two mana a turn off one card when you need it — but each untap costs a -1/-1 counter, so it shrinks toward its own grave. Milk it on the big turn, not every turn.
card_roles.Scaled Nurturer: Read the fine print: the 2 life needs a Dragon spell, and this deck casts none. It is a {G} dork with a dead clause — count it as mana and a body, nothing more.
card_roles.Elvish Spirit Guide: Free mana from your hand, any time. This is how a window you look tapped-out for still produces a Frostfang — the bluff the table cannot price.
card_roles.Tireless Provisioner: Every land drop banks a Treasure, and banked mana is exactly what a deck spending on other players' turns wants. Take Treasure over Food unless you are dying.
card_roles.Sakura-Tribe Elder: Chump-block, then become a Forest. Trading it into a 6/6 costs the attacker a swing and costs you nothing — the deck's whole posture in one card. Flashed on the end step before your turn, it even wakes up attack-ready (stack 006).
card_roles.Wood Elves: The metronome's poster card: {G} on an opponent's end step, and the fetched Forest enters untapped — all of it verified in stack 001. Body, land, window: one card.
card_roles.Cultivate: One land tapped now, one in hand for the drop you would otherwise miss — land drops fall to 56% by turn six, and this is the patch.
card_roles.Kodama's Reach: Cultivate's twin. Cast it on your own turn — it is one of the few cards here that insists.
card_roles.Rampant Growth: Two mana, one tapped Forest. It is the turn-two play when the hand has no dork.
card_roles.Three Visits: Rampant Growth, except the Forest enters untapped — a real difference in a deck that wants {G}{G} open on everyone else's turn.
card_roles.Elvish Reclaimer: A one-drop that fetches Boseiju or Castle Garenbrig the turn you need them, and wears +2/+2 once three lands hit the graveyard. Satyr Wayfinder and Life from the Loam feed it.
card_roles.Satyr Wayfinder: Digs four for a land and stocks the graveyard that Elvish Reclaimer and Life from the Loam want full. The 1/1 is the tip, not the product.
card_roles.Life from the Loam: Three lands back for two mana, forever, and dredge turns dead draws into fuel. This is the card that makes missing land drops optional.
card_roles.Utopia Sprawl: One mana that makes a Forest tap for two, from turn one. The sim models no auras at all, so every mana figure you have read is a floor this card quietly beats.
card_roles.Wild Growth: Same job as Utopia Sprawl on any land: one mana, and a land taps for two for the rest of the game.
card_roles.Fertile Ground: The two-mana copy of Wild Growth. Put it on the land you tap every turn.
card_roles.Beast Whisperer: A card per creature spell, and this deck casts one per window — up to four draws a round. Stack 003 shows it collecting even on the Craterhoof turn. Protect it accordingly.
card_roles.Toski, Bearer of Secrets: Cannot be countered, cannot be destroyed, must attack — and every connect anywhere on your team is a card. He skipped the wrath in stack 004 and shrugged off 6 damage in stack 002. Send him at the open seat every turn; that is what the must-attack clause is for.
card_roles.Selvala, Heart of the Wilds: The best engine card in the 99 and a class of exactly one — she shows up in 16% of games, so never plan around her. When she lands, a new biggest body draws its controller a card (usually you, with 35 creatures) and she taps for X equal to your greatest power. Chord of Calling fetches her at X=3 on the end step before yours, and she taps on your turn (stack 007).
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for everyone and a card per 4-power body entering. The static trample turns ordinary attacks into damage that always lands somewhere.
card_roles.Elemental Bond: A card per 3-power body entering. The dorks miss the bar; the middleweights clear it. Cast it before the bodies, not after — it only sees entries.
card_roles.Tribute to the World Tree: Never dead: a body with power 3+ draws, a smaller one takes two counters. Its {G}{G}{G} is the deck's heaviest cost, and 45 green sources make it routine.
card_roles.Fecundity: The wrath insurance, verified end to end: under Day of Judgment it drew you four and the wrath's caster one (stack 004). It is symmetric, so put it down when your board is the widest at the table and let everyone else fund your rebuild.
card_roles.Harmonize: Three cards, no conditions, no board required. It is the gas you cast on the turn the metronome has nothing worth flashing.
card_roles.Return of the Wildspeaker: An instant: end-step draw equal to your biggest non-Human power — the hoof makes that five, a grown Whiptongue Hydra more — or +3/+3 to the team as a second overrun mode. Radagast, the Hydra, and the hoof are all non-Human.
card_roles.Inspiring Call: Draws off +1/+1 counters and grants the counter-carriers indestructible at instant speed — Tribute to the World Tree and Warg Tactics load it. A wrath answer that pays you.
card_roles.Ohran Frostfang: The flagship trap: flashed after blockers are declared, it hands your attackers deathtouch in time for damage — a 1/1 killed a 6/6 on the record (stack 002) — and every connect draws a card. Hold three mana and the table must price it into every block.
card_roles.Guardian Augmenter: Flash it in response to the kill spell: Radagast becomes a hexproof 4/7 and stays one. The whole deck is linear on his window — this is the insurance premium, pre-paid.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: The pivot's seatbelt. Hold it for the turn you commit the board — hexproof and indestructible through the wrath they were saving.
card_roles.Tyvar's Stand: Intervention for one creature with an {X} attached: X=0 protects Radagast for one mana, X=5 turns a blocked trade into a kill. The trap mana you keep open is also this.
card_roles.Veil of Summer: One mana that beats a counterspell, a kill spell, or a discard spell out of the blue and black seats — and draws a card doing it. Against those decks, the cheapest insurance in the 99.
card_roles.Sylvan Safekeeper: A land for a shroud, any time, no mana. The removal-proof board costs you land drops — Life from the Loam buys them back.
card_roles.Beast Within: Any permanent, instant speed, three mana. The 3/3 they get is real, so aim it at the combo piece or the lock, where a Beast is a bargain.
card_roles.Pick Your Poison: One mana, and every opponent sacrifices an artifact, an enchantment, or a flyer — pick the mode that hits all three seats at once.
card_roles.Warg Tactics: Kill a flyer, or put a counter on your creature with trample and hexproof attached. The second mode feeds Inspiring Call and saves a body mid-combat.
card_roles.Caustic Caterpillar: A one-mana body holding a Disenchant. Cast it in a spare window and let it sit — the threat of activation taxes every artifact at the table.
card_roles.Nantuko Vigilante: Morph: a face-down 2/2 that flips for {1}{G} to eat an artifact or enchantment exactly when the target shows. The table never knows which trap the facedown is.
card_roles.Wickerbough Elder: It enters a 3/3 and grows to 4/4 by destroying an artifact or enchantment — removal that leaves a body behind. Take the counter off only when there is something worth killing.
card_roles.Collector Ouphe: Activated abilities of artifacts stop, and the Sol Ring seats lose their rocks. Mind the friendly fire: your own Treasures and Food go dark too. Cast it when their artifacts matter more than Tireless Provisioner's.
card_roles.Mirkwood Pathmaker: Power and toughness equal to your lands: modest when it arrives, a 7/7 by the pivot. Cheap now, big exactly when Craterhoof asks how big.
card_roles.Scute Swarm: Every land is a body, and past six lands every land is another Scute Swarm. This is where the fifth body comes from — and stack 003 says the fifth body is the difference between 36 and lethal.
card_roles.Eternal Witness: Buys back whatever the game took: the countered finisher, the spent Intervention, the dead Frostfang. A metronome body with a receipt.
card_roles.Fauna Shaman: A spare body in, the exact card out, every turn — with 35 creatures the discard is never a real cost. Loop toward Craterhoof when the board says pivot, toward Caustic Caterpillar when it says stop.
card_roles.Chord of Calling: Any body, instant speed, and convoke lets the board pay for its own reinforcement. Know what it refuses (stack 007): no Radagast discount — though the window survives untouched — no Castle Garenbrig six, no Beast Whisperer draw, and the fetched creature arrives uncast, triggering nothing that reads "cast."
card_roles.Craterhoof Behemoth: The pivot button, and the record is precise about pressing it: cast him in your own precombat main — X counts itself, and five bodies before him is exactly 40 trample into one seat, while four leaves a survivor at 4 (stacks 005, 003). Flashed on an end step, the pump dies at that turn's cleanup: flash him only to dodge a wrath, never to attack.
card_roles.Overwhelming Stampede: The second hoof: trample plus +X/+X where X is your greatest power, so any 5-power body makes it a team-wide +5. This is the finisher redundancy the pivot math demands.
card_roles.Pathbreaker Ibex: Craterhoof on a repeating trigger: every attack, trample and +X/+X off your biggest power. Protect it the turn before the pivot, not after.
card_roles.Boseiju, Who Endures: A Forest that answers an artifact, an enchantment, or a nonbasic land at instant speed — and your legends discount it, so with Radagast out Channel costs {G}. Fetch it with Elvish Reclaimer the moment the table shows a target.
card_roles.Castle Garenbrig: Six green in one activation, spendable only on creature spells and creature abilities — it pays for Craterhoof, never for Chord of Calling. Untapped as long as you control a Forest, which is always.
card_roles.Gemstone Mine: Three activations, then it sacrifices itself, and the any-colour clause buys nothing in mono-green. Treat it as a short-term untapped source and spend it early.
card_roles.Khalni Garden: Enters tapped and pays you a 0/1 Plant — a chump block, a convoke tapper, and a body under Craterhoof's X on a stalled board.
card_roles.Slippery Karst: A tapped Forest early, a fresh card for {2} late. Cycle it the moment land drops stop mattering.
card_roles.Thriving Grove: Enters tapped, and the colour it names is wasted here. Sequence it on a turn you were not spending anyway.
card_roles.Forest: Thirty copies — enough that Wood Elves, Three Visits, Utopia Sprawl, and Castle Garenbrig's untapped clause never miss.
card_roles.Bala Ged Recovery // Bala Ged Sanctuary: A land when you need the drop, a Regrowth when you need the card back — the tapped-land mode is the price of never being dead. Default to the land side early; the recovery side exists for the finisher the graveyard is holding.
card_roles.Arasta of the Endless Web: Every instant or sorcery an opponent casts hands you a 1/2 reach Spider — width that accrues on other people's turns, which is the only kind of turn this deck respects. Against the spellslinger seat she is a body per spell; against everyone she is reach the flyers must price.
card_roles.Hornet Nest: A 0/2 nobody sane touches: every point of damage it takes becomes that many 1/1 flying deathtouch Insects. It cannot attack — it sat out both swings in stack 005 — so its whole job is making your half of the board a minefield.
card_roles.Dawn's Light Archer: A trap with the flash printed on: a 4/2 reach body that ambushes a flyer mid-combat without spending Radagast's window. Power 4 fires Garruk's Uprising on the way in.
card_roles.Saryth, the Viper's Fang: Read her two halves by tap state: your tapped creatures — the attackers — all have deathtouch, and your untapped ones at home hide behind hexproof. The {1}, {T} untap is a lever: reset Selvala, or move a body from one gift to the other.
card_roles.Deathgorge Scavenger: The 99's only answer to an opponent's graveyard — everything else here that touches a graveyard recurs your own cards — and it exiles on entry and again on every attack. A power-3 body besides, so Elemental Bond and Tribute pay out on arrival.
card_roles.Hornet Queen: Five bodies from one card — the biggest single jump toward the five the kill math demands — and all five fly with deathtouch, so the same card is your insurance against a mass attack. Seven mana at retail, {2}{G}{G}{G} in a Radagast window.
card_roles.Ravenous Sailback: A modal trap on a power-4 body: cast in your own main, the haste mode makes a surprise attacker; flashed into a window, the other mode eats an artifact or enchantment. Either way it is never dead, and power 4 pays the Garruk's Uprising toll.
card_roles.Whiptongue Hydra: The board reset the deck owns, aimed straight up: it enters, every flier dies, and it grows a +1/+1 counter per kill. Six mana at retail, {3}{G} in a window — hold it for the flyer table and it lands as a reach wall the size of what it killed.
card_roles.Glademuse: A card for every spell cast off-turn — and read it honestly: everyone's off-turn casts, not just yours. You cast on other people's turns for a living and the table mostly doesn't, so the symmetry leans your way; against an instant-speed seat it feeds them too.
card_roles.Yeva, Nature's Herald: She lifts the cap: while she's out, every green creature spell you cast has flash, so Radagast's once-per-turn clause binds only the discount. A 4/4 with flash herself — the second, third, and fourth body can now all arrive on someone else's end step.
card_roles.Indrik Stomphowler: A 4/4 that eats an artifact or enchantment on arrival, joining Nantuko Vigilante, Wickerbough Elder, and Ravenous Sailback in the answer class that walks. Flash it into a window and the Disenchant comes at instant speed.

mulligan:
Keep two to four lands and one accelerant — that is the whole rule, and the sim backs it: 81.5% of first sevens are keeps, and kept hands cluster at two to four lands. A one-mana dork is turn-three Radagast; he lands on three in about a third of games and on four in more than half, nearly always off an Elves.

The second thing to want is something to do at instant speed: an Ohran Frostfang, a Heroic Intervention, a Wood Elves to flash into someone's end step. A hand that plays draw-go from turn three is a keep. A hand that must tap out on its own turn every turn is playing someone else's deck.

Ship three shapes. Two or more five-plus drops — Craterhoof Behemoth is the payoff, not the plan. All lands and dorks with nothing to hold up. And any hand you are keeping because Selvala, Heart of the Wilds is in it — she is a class of one, so she is a bonus, never a reason. Everything else, keep: this deck averages 0.22 mulligans, and it earns that by not needing much.
upgrades:
Five is the number the kill needs, and 3.8 is the average board at turn six — the bar is crossed only around turn eight, at 5.3. That gap is still the binding constraint: the diagnosis walks sixteen axes and finds the mana over-supplied, the ambush machinery near-universal, and board width the number every other weakness sits downstream of. The Short List's first job is bodies.

One board reset lives in the 99 and it reads only the sky: Whiptongue Hydra, a wipe for fliers that leaves everything on the ground standing. A resolved wide ground board still has no answer here — the diagnosis's own open question names Ezuri's Predation as the better shape for a board this creature-dense, filed threat:tokens where the sweeper axis cannot see it.

The back of the list is doors, not deficits. Seedborn Muse is a recorded Game Changer: adding her moves the computed floor to exactly the target. The two-card-infinite pair — Nissa, Resurgent Animist with Springheart Nantuko, and Springheart with Tireless Provisioner, already aboard — is the bracket-4 conversation, and it is a table conversation, not a deckbuilding one.

Inside the bracket, the thin classes hold their shape: a finisher is in hand by turn six in 42.4% of games, assembled with its second wave in 40.2%, and Selvala, Heart of the Wilds remains a class of one at 16%. Width first, the ground sweeper second, redundancy third — the numbers keep that order.
mana_base:
Thirty-six land copies across seven names, and thirty of them say Forest. Four enter tapped, three of those unconditionally — an 11% tap rate against the usual one-in-three budget, about as far under budget as a manabase gets. The colour ledger is one line long: pip share 1.00, source share 1.00. Mono-green leaves nothing to arbitrate.

The target says G36 and the lands supply exactly 36 — met on the nose before the nine creature-side producers lift the total to 45. Lands alone put the deck on curve 90.6% of the time; count the dorks and it is 97%. Eighty-two green pips across 63 cards, and nothing asks for more than three at once — the triple-{G} costs, Tribute to the World Tree, Hornet Queen, and Craterhoof Behemoth, are what the 45 exist for.

What the dorks actually buy is the commander's clock. Mean available mana reaches 4.14 on turn four; Radagast costs four, and his mean cast is turn 4.0. Land drops decay from 91% on turn three to 56% by turn six, which is why the back half of the ramp package is shaped like recovery — Life from the Loam, Satyr Wayfinder, and the Cultivate pair's land-in-hand.

Two footnotes the figures cannot show. Castle Garenbrig's six-mana burst spends only on creature spells and creature abilities, and the record settles it both ways: it pays for a flashed Craterhoof (stack 005) and never for Chord of Calling (stack 007). And the three ramp auras appear in neither the hypergeometrics nor the goldfish arithmetic, so every number above is a floor: this manabase measures better than it reads, and it already reads clean.
editors_letter:
The moment this deck produces that I had not expected is not a moment on your turn.

It is the pause. The player to your left, mana up, looking at your untapped Forests and deciding — visibly, slowly — to attack somebody else instead. Radagast of Rhosgobel makes the first creature spell you cast each turn cost less and lets you cast it as though it had flash, and "each turn" turns out to mean everyone's turn. Counselor Dictum has the ruling on that, and it holds: four windows a round, three of them on other people's clocks. This deck is built around the three turns you don't get.

What made it worth an issue is that the payoff has an exact edge, and two of our verified scenarios found that edge from opposite sides — one board that does not kill, one board that does, a single creature apart. The panel spends most of the log arguing about that creature. Ledger has how often you find it. The Counselor has the harder news: the Craterhoof was never the thing you were counting.

You will have a good time here if you like being the seat nobody wants to test, if you would rather hold two mana than spend six, and if the word "combo" plays no part in your idea of a good evening. You will not, if you want to tap out and see what happens. This deck asks you to sit still with your hands full.

Ledger ran the draws. The Counselor read the rules. Nobody on this masthead has yet played a game with it — which is not a disclaimer, it is an invitation.

pilots_log.text:
Turn seven. Radagast of Rhosgobel is out, Scute Swarm and Wood Elves and Beast Whisperer beside him, six Forests untapped, and you have just drawn Craterhoof Behemoth. Your hand is already reaching.

Put it back down.

I have watched this exact board go off and I have watched it fall short, and the difference between them is not a land and it is not a better target. It is one creature. You are four across. You need five before the Hoof lands, because the Hoof counts itself and then the whole board swings, and what comes out the other end is either a dead player or a story about how close you got.

Count the board. Then swing.

The Coach is right, and I would like the record to show how narrowly.

Stack 003 is his exact board — Radagast, Scute Swarm, Wood Elves, Beast Whisperer, and Craterhoof cast in your own precombat main. X is 5. The creatures come out at 7, 6, 6, 7 and 10, they all attack one open seat, and the total is 36 into 40 life. That player survives at 4. Beast Whisperer draws you a card on the way past, which is a consolation and not a kill.

Stack 005 asks the same question over a five-body board. X is 6, the board swings for 40 trampling power, and the seat is dead with nothing left over. Not thirty-nine. Not forty-two. Forty.

So the threshold is proved rather than asserted, and the thing that crosses it is not the Craterhoof. It is the fifth body. The finisher is the card the table remembers; the body is the card that decided it.

Bodies on board, ten thousand seeded runs: 3.77 at turn six, 4.59 at turn seven, 5.31 at turn eight. The Counselor's bar is five other bodies. The median game clears it on turn eight.

A mass-pump finisher is drawn by turn six in 42.4% of runs. The assembled figure this deck's file quotes is 40.2%, and the label wants reading out loud before anyone spends it: that group asks for a finisher plus ONE other body. It is measuring the board stack 003 says survives.

Three things the simulator does not model — the commander's cost reduction, the ramp auras, and casting on an opponent's turn. Those three are the deck. So the rates above are floors, and the size of the gap is unmeasured.

Five. Say it out loud at the table if that's what it takes.

And here's the part that wins you a game you were going to lose: the fifth body does not have to attack. Hornet Nest has defender. It blocks, it sits there, it never swings — and it still makes the Hoof bigger for everybody standing next to it. Same goes for whatever you flashed in on the end step before.

Bodies count. Attackers deal. You are not hunting for a fifth attacker, you are hunting for a fifth creature, and those are different searches with different answers.

Which brings me to the temptation, since the Coach has raised the end step.

You will want to flash the Craterhoof in on the turn before yours. It is legal — stack 005 verifies the entire cast, including Castle Garenbrig's six restricted green paying for a discounted Hoof, which is the one place in this deck that land is worth exactly what it looks like. The trigger resolves. Your creatures get +6/+6 and trample.

Then rule 514.2 takes all of it away at that turn's cleanup, before your turn has begun. You untap into an unpumped board and attack for ten.

The holding, in plain English: the ambush Hoof is a way to deploy at the last moment a sorcery-speed wrath can reach you, and nothing more. It is not the kill. The kill is cast in your own precombat main, where the pump and your combat phase live in the same turn.

Take that one to heart, because it feels wonderful and it does nothing.

Flash the Hoof when somebody has four mana open, a white deck, and a face that says wrath. That is the only time. Otherwise he lands on your own turn, first main, and you attack with him.

Everything else, though — flash everything else. That is the job. Three of the four turns in a round are not yours and this deck gets a discounted creature in each of them. Pass with mana up and let the player to your left decide whether finding out is worth it. Put a body down in somebody's end step and it wakes up able to attack and able to tap. You are not durdling. You are building the board on other people's clocks so your own turn stays free for the swing.

On the mana that pays for that. Mean available at turn six: 5.50. Land drop hit rate at turn six: 56.5%. 36 lands, 36 green sources, on curve at 90.6% on lands alone and 97.0% once the dorks are counted.

Commander down: mean turn 4.02, 94.1% by turn six. Keep-seven rate 81.5%, mean mulligans 0.22.

One figure to set beside the rest. Selvala, Heart of the Wilds is drawn by turn six in 12.3% of runs, and she is the one-card class in the declaration — the label beside her states that no backup exists in the 99. Stack 007 finds her with Chord of Calling at instant speed. The hypergeometric is right and the sentence next to it is not.

Since we are quoting the record, here is what is on it about those three turns.

Stack 001: Wood Elves cast on an opponent's turn for one green, because it was the first creature spell you cast that turn — your cast on your own earlier turn belonged to a different turn. "Each turn" means each player's. One window per turn, first spell only, four a round in a four-player pod.

Stack 006: a body flashed on the end step before yours satisfies both prongs of rule 302.6 by your untap. It may attack and it may tap. End-step flash is haste with better timing.

Stack 002: Ohran Frostfang arriving after blockers are declared applies deathtouch to damage already lined up, and one unblocked 1/1 then draws exactly two.

And the boundary, which is the part of this deck I enjoy most. Stack 007: Chord of Calling takes no discount, consumes no window, cannot be paid with Garenbrig's restricted mana, and triggers no Beast Whisperer — it is an instant, and the creature it finds is put onto the battlefield rather than cast. All of that verified. The commander is generous to creature spells and to nothing else in the deck.

Then let me ask the question the reader is holding. Five bodies are down, it is my turn, and the card in my hand is Overwhelming Stampede instead of the Hoof.

Swing. Pathbreaker Ibex, Return of the Wildspeaker, I don't much mind which one turned up — you run four finishers precisely so that one of them turns up. Take the shot.

No. Or more exactly: possibly, and I will not let you say it as though anyone knew.

Craterhoof Behemoth is the only one of the four that counts creatures. Overwhelming Stampede and Pathbreaker Ibex multiply by the greatest power among your creatures, and Return of the Wildspeaker is a flat +3/+3 with no trample that touches only your non-Human creatures — and this deck runs three Humans it will therefore skip. Over a board of 1/1s those are not one card, and none of them is producing the Hoof's number. Half of them cannot even use the window: the commander reduces creature spells, and a sorcery and an instant are neither.

Not one passing stack in this deck resolves Stampede, Ibex or Return. So I can tell you what the cards say and I cannot tell you what they deal, and "nobody has checked yet" is the whole of the honest sentence.

It applies to something larger, too. Eight cards in this deck exist so that one removal spell is not the entire game, and not one of them appears in the scenario of any passing stack. Saryth, the Viper's Fang protects OTHER untapped creatures — which is neither herself nor a commander who has attacked. Guardian Augmenter grants hexproof, which is not indestructible and does not survive a wrath. Both of those are readings of printed text. Neither is a ruling.

The rate gives him no cover either. 42.4% by turn six counts Craterhoof Behemoth, Overwhelming Stampede, Pathbreaker Ibex and Return of the Wildspeaker as one class of four interchangeable cards. It was built to price a draw, not a kill. Split the four and three of them have no figure at all.

The insurance is the same shape: eight cards, zero passing stacks. There is no rate to report there. Not a small one — none.

All right. I'll take it. Both of them.

So here is your game. Pass with mana open and make three players wonder. Put a body down in somebody else's end step whenever you can pay for it. Count to five — five creatures beside the finisher, and one of them is allowed to be a Hornet Nest that will never attack anybody. Then untap, cast Craterhoof Behemoth in your first main, and send the board at the seat that cannot block it.

And when the card in your hand is one of the other three, you make that call yourself, at the table, with the Counselor's warning in your ear. That is not a hole in the plan. That is the part of the game that is still yours.
